newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia tightens grip ahead of May elections.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia tightens grip ahead of May elections.

text.p: The Indonesian government has further tightened its grip on political activity ahead of May 29 general elections, saying officials will vet speeches broadcast on television and radio during the pre-poll campaign.

"A team which includes officials from the Home Affairs and Information Ministries will screen the speeches before they are broadcast...," an official of the election committee overseeing the elections said on Wednesday.
Political broadcasts are made over state television and radio and relayed on private networks.

The official said political speeches from the three parties legally permitted to contest the national and local elections should not attack the government and should stick to the programmes of the respective political groups.
"In addition to the screening, campaigners should also hold a police permit to make speeches at public gatherings during the election campaign," he added.

Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, meanwhile, said a U.S. State Department report last week accusing Indonesia of serious human rights abuses and of intimidating political opponents ahead of the elections was exaggerated.
"There are many things in the report which, we believe, have been exaggerated," he told reporters before a cabinet meeting. He said the government would respond to the report, but he did not amplify.

The election commission spokesman said the broadcasting order was sent on Tuesday to the three legal parties, the ruling Golkar, the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI).

The campaign runs from April 27 to May 23, followed by a five-day cooling off period before Indonesians vote for 425 seats in the 500-seat national legislature. The military, whose members do not vote, names the other 75 legislators.
Golkar won 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI -- now riven by internal disputes -- 15 percent.

The broadcast regulation is the latest in a series of restrictions ordered by a government shaken by a series of recent riots in different parts of the sprawling archipelago with a population of 200 million.
The Home Affairs Ministry has told local governments to restrict major public gatherings ahead of the elections to lower the risk of violence.
The election committee spokesman said each of the political parties would be allowed to have a 15-minute broadcast to be delivered by the party chairman.
"The parties are also entitled to have a public debate which lasts for 30 minutes," he added.

The official Antara news agency reported on Wednesday that campaigning advertisements were banned, while the government would also regulate posters, banners, brochures and other campaign aids. It gave no details.
The Home Affairs Ministry has also ordered all organisations to postpone large-scale meetings or seminars until after the elections to avoid potential disturbances.
